info.desc: In Utero is the third and final studio album by the American alternative rock band Nirvana, released on September 21, 1993 by DGC Records. Following the success of the group's 1991 breakthrough album Nevermind, Nirvana sought to avoid that album's polished production and hired recording engineer Steve Albini to produce the record. The band recorded In Utero with Albini in two weeks in February 1993, capturing an abrasive and naturalistic sound for the record. While some of the songs had been written years prior, the lyrics largely dealt with frontman Kurt Cobain's reflections on his newfound fame and recent personal .

It would be released that September."

podcast.body: Nirvana (specifically Kurt Cobain) chose Steve Albini to produce their third album, *In Utero*, because he had previously produced *Surfer Rosa* by Pixies and *Pod* by The Breeders, two of their favorite records. Albini's specific technical approach, which involved capturing natural room ambiance with strategically placed microphones, had been rejected by previous producers but was essential to Nirvana, leading them to insist on his services. "Corco vain quiso Steve Alvini para producir su tercer álbum minútero."

podcast.body: Recorded in mid-February 1993, Kurt Cobain was determined to make this album "rawness and raggedness" in sound, explicitly as an "FU song for the record called Radio Friendly Unit Shifter" to the expectation of another *Nevermind*. Steve Albini was chosen to record it for his "ragged and raw" style. The record label, DGC Records, was "upset" with early samples, claiming poor songwriting and an "un-listenable" mix, fearing its release. The album's final mix was modified from Albini's original due to label pressure, though Kurt "hated what was eventually released officially." Initial first week sales were 180,000 copies, considered "very, very light" compared to *Nevermind*. Major retailers Walmart and Kmart refused to stock the album due to its content not conforming to "family values." "For a while, there were doubts as to whether the album would ever be released."

podcast.body: The cover artwork for Nirvana's 1993 album *In Utero*, designed by Art Director Robert Fisher, features a winged figure on a pale, cracked background. This angelic figure is depicted as ripped open, exposing bare bones and organs, reflecting Kurt Cobain's fascination with human anatomy as art, creating an image that is both peaceful and disturbing. The figure is actually a "transparent anatomical mannequin," a life-sized, anatomically correct female model used for teaching anatomy, which was found at a medical supply store in the Mall of America in Minneapolis. Nirvana used several such mannequins as stage props for the *In Utero* tour. The back cover, photographed by Charles Peterson, displays various items from the medical store and Kurt's personal collection, including plastic fetuses, body parts, a turtle shell, orchids, and lilies, all laid out on his living room floor. These items incorporate symbols from *The Woman's Dictionary of Symbols and Sacred Objects*, aligning with Kurt's interest in artwork representing themes of sex, women, birth, and death, which also hints at the raw music within the album. "The angelic figure is ripped open. We see bare bones and exposed organs, but not to Kurt s fascination with human anatomy as art. It's both peaceful and disturbing."

Walmart stores notably refused to stock it due to its artwork and lyrical content, and fans were reportedly growing tired of Kurt's personal issues and anti-star persona. "When in Yudrow came out on the fall of 1993, it really kind of fizzled."
